title: Persistent mobile operations at full ocean depth

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an uncrewed scientific vehicle that can work routinely across the ocean’s depth range, including the deepest trenches, for a seasonal campaign. It would combine sustained operation, movement between sites, repeat navigation, useful scientific measurements or sampling, and reliable recovery and reuse. The defining advance is the combination: reaching great depth alone does not demonstrate persistent mobile access.

Concept synthesis: such a vehicle would let researchers maintain a mobile scientific presence without a ship continuously holding station overhead. A campaign could follow changes through time, survey a trench, return to an instrument or sampling location, and bring back calibrated records or samples. This is a proposed operational capability; the supplied evidence does not demonstrate its complete realization or establish its worldwide availability.

significance.text: If achieved with dependable reuse and affordable campaign costs, seasonal mobile access would substantially change how scientists investigate the deepest ocean. Suitable sensors would enable sustained ecological and physical time series, while repeat navigation would support revisits and repeated sampling. These capabilities would extend the baseline observations and follow-up investigations motivated by the Alvin account and the 2025 trench-community study. Instrument servicing and manipulative experiments would additionally require appropriate tools, payloads, measurement controls and intervention capability.

The scientific opportunity includes observing how trench ecosystems and physical conditions change between expedition visits. Peng and colleagues’ discovery of extensive chemosynthesis-based communities illustrates the importance of these environments, and their paper identifies a need to revisit seeps with focused coring and drilling. Persistent access could help organize and contextualize such follow-up work, although a mobile observing vehicle would not automatically possess drilling or coring capability.

Impact synthesis: better ecological explanations, improved trench-circulation models and new discoveries would be downstream research outcomes, conditional on suitable measurements, sampling design and analysis. They are not guaranteed consequences of endurance or mobility. The useful analogy is a shift from intermittent expeditions toward a recurring scientific workplace, but autonomy would still depend on maintenance, deployment and recovery infrastructure, payload capacity and explicit operating limits. A season-long vehicle would not by itself provide simultaneous coverage of the whole ocean.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability defined by this proposal is the reliable integration of seasonal endurance, mobility, repeat visits and routine reuse at full ocean depth. The supplied sources establish severe environmental conditions and limited numbers of vehicles capable of abyssal and hadal access. They also document vehicles reaching great depth. They do not provide a comprehensive assessment of worldwide endurance, station-keeping or autonomous operational capability, so they cannot establish that the proposed combination is presently absent everywhere.

Engineering synthesis: a convincing system would have to maintain pressure integrity and reliable propulsion, buoyancy control, electronics and scientific payloads through prolonged exposure and repeated deployment cycles. Its energy budget would need to cover movement, sensing, computation and communication throughout the declared mission. Navigation would need to support both travel and independently measured returns to earlier sites. Communication and onboard autonomy would need to accommodate whatever contact with external infrastructure the operating protocol permits. These are concrete requirements implied by the target capability, not a source-verified diagnosis of the dominant failure modes of every existing vehicle.

Engineering synthesis: persistence also requires managing faults, sensor drift, sample integrity and safe recovery over a campaign long enough for small failures to accumulate. Routine reuse demands evidence about turnaround, maintenance burden and performance on subsequent deployments. The earlier approximately 110 MPa figure and categorical statements about radio and GPS are not established by the supplied review; the supported environmental description is immense pressure, cold and absence of sunlight in the deep environments under discussion. No feasibility date follows from this record.

current_state.text: Rubin, Michel and Soule’s Eos article, dated 31 January 2025 in the reviewed article text, reports that upgraded Alvin can reach 6,500 m, providing access to roughly 99% of the ocean floor by area. It describes successful verification dives in 2022 and subsequent operations exceeding 100 dives per year. The article also identifies the small number of abyssal- and hadal-capable vehicles as a constraint on exploration. These are substantial demonstrated access and operational achievements, but neither the area percentage nor annual dive count demonstrates seasonal uncrewed mobility at approximately 11,000 m.

The earlier research attributes to a 2023 Petrel-X PLUS paper three dives exceeding 10,000 m, a maximum depth of 10,619 m and average station-keeping accuracy of 2.018 km. It separately attributes a design range of 80 dives or 200 days. These figures remain unverified in the supplied review because the retained DOI artifact contains only redirect text, with no usable abstract or article content. If confirmed, the three dives would describe a trial, whereas 80 dives or 200 days would describe a design claim rather than demonstrated endurance. The meaning and measurement basis of the station-keeping figure also require the underlying paper. The access limitation is not evidence that the reported results are false.

The earlier notes use a 2018 Jamieson paper to frame the hadal zone as approximately 6,000–11,000 m and as a remaining frontier. The reviewed copy contains only redirect text, so that attribution and depth definition cannot be verified from it. Similarly, the notes attribute to Glud and Schauberger’s 2024 Forum article an account of trenches concentrating deposited organic matter and an estimated 70-fold greater organic-carbon sequestration per unit area than abyssal-plain sediments. Its retained DOI copy also contains only redirect text. The 70-fold estimate therefore remains an unresolved attributed claim, not an established quantitative premise for this innovation; the qualitative organic-matter pathway in the Nature study does not independently verify that ratio.

Peng, Du, Gebruk and colleagues’ Nature paper, published online on 30 July 2025, reports findings from the TS42 expedition conducted between 7 July and 18 August 2024 using the human-occupied submersible Fendouzhe. The paper describes Fendouzhe as capable of reaching nearly 11,000 m. Its abstract reports chemosynthesis-based communities extending across 2,500 km in the Kuril–Kamchatka and western Aleutian trenches, at an attributed depth range of 5,800–9,533 m, and presents them as the deepest and most extensive such communities then known. This was a crewed expedition, not a demonstration of seasonal autonomous presence. The reviewed text does not establish individual dive durations.

The Nature study connects these communities to sulfide-rich and methane-rich fluids and reports isotopic evidence that methane was produced microbially from deposited organic matter. Its formation model connects that material to productive surface waters and transport by gravity flows. Chemosynthesis here therefore does not establish a trench-wide metabolism independent of surface-derived organic matter. Contrary to the earlier abstract-only description, the supplied review had access to the article’s main text and Methods. The abstract’s depth range should nevertheless remain explicitly attributed: Supplementary Table 1 lists seep ranges including 9,554–9,570 m and 5,662–5,743 m, outside the abstract’s endpoints. The precise relationship between these seep ranges and the community-depth claim remains unreconciled.

Taken together, the documented vehicle operations and biological discoveries establish meaningful deep-ocean access and scientific opportunity. They do not establish the complete proposed operational capability, and they do not prove its worldwide nonexistence as of 1 November 2026. The supplied freshness record contains no bounded current capability search. The remaining uncertainty is therefore both technical and evidential: feasibility, timeline and the present worldwide frontier cannot be resolved from these dated examples alone.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: an uncrewed vehicle operates as ordinary scientific equipment for at least one seasonal cycle, with actual operation at hadal depths and qualification across the surface-to-approximately-11,000 m range. During the campaign it surveys on the order of tens of kilometers, returns to a previously visited site within a declared tolerance of order 100 m, and delivers calibrated sensor records or samples with documented scientific integrity. These numbers are proposed targets, not established standards, published performance requirements or evidence of feasibility.
completion_criteria.label: Seasonal mobile scientific operations demonstrate surface-to-approximately-11,000 m capability

completion_criteria.text: Proposed protocol: define the seasonal duration, total mission duration and submerged endurance separately. State permitted surfacing, ship assistance, external navigation aids, communication infrastructure and any resupply or servicing. Identify how much operation must occur at hadal depth, how the full depth range is qualified, and how survey distance and revisit error are measured. A claimed return within 100 m should be checked against an independent positional reference with stated uncertainty rather than solely against the vehicle’s own navigation estimate.
completion_criteria.label: Declared campaign protocol includes independently referenced 100 m revisit verification

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility test: repeat deployments should demonstrate recovery, turnaround and reuse, with mission logs, calibration records, interventions, failures and maintenance requirements available for assessment. Scientific outputs should be evaluated against declared data-quality or sample-quality requirements. Independent assessment and, where feasible, replication by another operating team would make the result more convincing than a single exceptional expedition. A finite campaign would establish performance across its tested depths, terrain, currents, payloads and operating conditions; it would not establish literal operation anywhere in the ocean.
completion_criteria.label: Repeat deployments demonstrate recovery, reuse and assessed scientific output quality

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical benchmark: compare campaign cost and reliability with a named contemporary upper-ocean autonomous campaign using declared accounting and success measures. Include deployment and recovery, ship time, external infrastructure, personnel, maintenance and losses, alongside useful scientific output. Cost parity is an aspiration to test, not a demonstrated property. Instrument servicing, coring, drilling or manipulative experiments should count as achieved only when the relevant payload functions are separately demonstrated.
completion_criteria.label: Campaign cost and reliability benchmarked against named upper-ocean autonomous operations

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: OCE-02, Synoptic sensing of the ocean interior, overlaps in observation and vehicle deployment, but concerns broad spatial coverage and coordinated measurements. OCE-04 concerns sustained mobile access at full depth; one persistent vehicle would not deliver synoptic ocean coverage. OCE-10, Basin-scale underwater positioning without surfacing, could contribute navigation infrastructure or methods, but a local revisit demonstration does not establish basin-scale positioning. Conversely, basin-scale positioning alone does not supply endurance, full-depth qualification or useful payload operations.

Roster-based synthesis: OCE-08, Continuous centimeter-level geodesy of the seismogenic seafloor, overlaps through instrument deployment, servicing and repeat visits. Its measurement objective is distinct from vehicle navigation: OCE-04’s proposed order-100-m revisit tolerance is not centimeter-level geodesy. A mobile vehicle might support a geodetic observing network, but would not by itself demonstrate continuous deformation measurements.

Roster-based synthesis: OCE-03, A predictive closure of the biological carbon pump, could benefit from repeated observations and sampling of deep organic-matter deposition and transformation. OCE-05, Closure of ocean–crust fluid and biogeochemical exchange, could benefit from access to fluid-release sites and repeated geochemical sampling. Neither predictive closure follows from access alone. In particular, the methane pathway reported in the supplied trench study involves deposited organic matter and should not automatically be treated as evidence of ocean–crust exchange.

Roster-based synthesis: OCE-01, A closed theory of oceanic turbulent transport, and OCE-07, The stability class of the global overturning circulation, could use relevant physical observations gathered by full-depth platforms. Their central goals remain theoretical and system-level inference, requiring appropriate measurements, models and spatial coverage beyond a vehicle demonstration. OCE-04 supplies a possible means of obtaining observations rather than either theoretical result.

Roster-based synthesis: OCE-06, A verified law of ice-shelf basal melting, shares a need for sustained access to difficult environments, but full-depth ocean qualification does not establish under-ice navigation, recovery or measurements sufficient to verify a melting law. OCE-09, A predictive theory of pelagic size structure and trophic transfer, could benefit from biological measurements during water-column transits, but seasonal trench access does not by itself resolve pelagic ecosystem dynamics. These remain separate innovations with distinct evidence requirements.

change_log.change: Preserved OCE-04’s identity while defining the innovation as the integrated combination of seasonal endurance, mobility, repeat navigation, scientific utility and routine reuse.

unresolved_issues: The supplied record does not establish whether the complete proposed capability is available anywhere worldwide as of 1 November 2026; no bounded freshness search is supplied.

Petrel-X PLUS authorship, trial figures, station-keeping metric and 80-dive/200-day design claim require usable article content. The review’s recommendation to remove these numbers entirely was not adopted because the requested record preserves unresolved quantitative detail; they remain explicitly unverified.

The Jamieson attribution and the Glud–Schauberger depocenter and 70-fold sequestration claims remain unverified. Although the research supplies an additional open-PDF URL for the latter, no corresponding reviewed content establishes that estimate.
The relationship between the Nature abstract’s 5,800–9,533 m community range and supplementary seep ranges of 5,662–5,743 m and 9,554–9,570 m remains unresolved.
The seasonal duration, required hadal operating time, permitted surfacing and external support, qualification protocol and independent revisit-error reference still need to be specified.
No named upper-ocean cost and reliability comparator, agreed accounting method or full-depth campaign feasibility estimate is supplied.
The supplied review does not establish individual Fendouzhe dive durations. Its distinction between expedition access and seasonal autonomy does not depend on calling those dives short.
The Eos magazine PDF has extraction gaps, but complete HTML supports the retained claims. No conclusion here depends on uninspected images or the textless Nature reporting-summary PDF.

brief.title: Season-long research across the ocean’s full depth
possible: Scientists could follow changes in the deepest trenches through a season without keeping a ship overhead. An uncrewed vehicle could travel between sites, return to earlier locations and bring back reliable measurements or samples.
Researchers could recover the vehicle and use it again, making repeated investigations part of routine scientific work.
why: Scientists would gain a continuing view of trench life and changing physical conditions between expeditions. Repeated visits would help them investigate how these environments work.

Seasonal observations could support better explanations of trench ecosystems and models of deep-ocean circulation. Extensive communities supported by chemical energy give researchers places to investigate over time.

shown: Alvin has demonstrated repeated crewed operations after an upgrade allowing dives to 6,500 metres. This establishes useful deep-ocean access, but does not demonstrate the proposed seasonal uncrewed capability.

Peng and colleagues used Fendouzhe to find communities supported by chemical energy along 2,500 kilometres of trench. Their work shows what deep expeditions can discover; it did not test persistent mobile operations.
missing: A seasonal campaign must combine full-depth operation, travel between sites, accurate returns and reliable scientific measurements or samples.
Power, navigation and scientific equipment must keep working through prolonged exposure, with faults managed and the vehicle recovered safely.
Repeated deployments must establish dependable reuse, manageable maintenance and consistent scientific quality.
Campaign costs and reliability must be compared with named autonomous operations in shallower waters.

milestones.label: Seasonal mobile science at full ocean depth
milestones.explanation: An uncrewed seasonal campaign would have to qualify operation down to about 11,000 metres, survey tens of kilometres, revisit sites accurately and deliver reliable measurements or samples. This would demonstrate the combined capability.

milestones.label: Independent checks confirm accurate returns under declared operating rules
milestones.explanation: A campaign would have to declare duration, deep-trench activity, support and measurement rules, with an independent reference checking returns within 100 metres. This would make its performance claim assessable.

milestones.label: Repeated deployments deliver recovery, reuse and reliable science
milestones.explanation: Repeated deployments would have to demonstrate recovery, turnaround, reuse and scientific quality, with failures and maintenance assessed independently. This would establish repeatable performance under the tested conditions.

milestones.label: Campaign costs and reliability withstand a practical comparison
milestones.explanation: Costs and reliability would have to be compared with a named shallower-water autonomous campaign, counting support and useful science, with added tools demonstrated separately. This would test practical value and claimed capabilities.

uncertain: The required season length, time in the deepest trenches and permitted surfacing, servicing and external support remain undefined.
The full combination’s feasibility and timeline remain uncertain.
The appropriate cost comparator and fair measures of reliability and scientific output remain unsettled.

page.title: Full-ocean-depth autonomous underwater vehicle campaigns
page.definition: An autonomous underwater vehicle, an uncrewed robot that navigates onboard, conducts a six-month mobile scientific deployment at the deepest trench floor, within an 11,000 m operating envelope. It revisits mapped sites, returns measurements or samples, and can be recovered and used again.

goal.need: Alvin's upgrade expanded seafloor access, but its depth limit excludes the deepest trenches. During TS42, from 7 July to 18 August 2024, Fendouzhe documented chemosynthetic communities on 19 of 23 dives along 2,500 km of trench. The study calls for return visits with focused coring and drilling; the National Academies recommend sustained autonomous observations.

figures.caption: Access provided by the upgraded crewed submersible Alvin.
figures.note: Depth capability and accessible area do not measure autonomous endurance.

statements.body: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
statements.quote: the increased use of autonomous assets for making sustained observations and increasing the efficiency of oceanographic expeditions
statements.context: Recommendation 4.4 identifies activities that NSF's Division of Ocean Sciences and its partners should explicitly support.

statements.quote: These are modular, relatively inexpensive, 11,000 meter depth rated AUVs which will enable systematic exploration of hadal depths.
statements.context: Approved EX-21-02 instructions describe the Orpheus vehicles and their intended scientific role. A depth rating is a design specification.

statements.quote: 6 months endurance at slow speeds with a low power payload.
statements.context: NOC's developers restate the original ALR6000 design target, which also specified a 6,000 m depth rating and 6,000 km range. They distinguish this target from the operational vehicle's reduced endurance.

completion.title: A full-depth AUV returns six months of mobile science data and completes a further full-depth mission.
completion.criterion: An 11,000 m-qualified AUV completes six months of mobile scientific operation at the Challenger Deep seabed, without servicing or continuous attendance by a ship. It moves between study sites and autonomously re-identifies a previously mapped site. Recovery returns measurements or samples that meet the scientific mission's published acceptance criteria. After recovery, the same vehicle completes a further scientific mission at Challenger Deep. The duration is adapted from NOC's 6,000 m vehicle design target; its extension to full depth and the reuse requirement are Atlas criteria.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; a synthesis of separately published depth, navigation and endurance objectives, without an external combined acceptance test.
completion.basis: No combined acceptance test was found in NOAA's Orpheus instructions, NASA/JPL's navigation goals, the National Academies' roadmap, ARPA-E's marine-platform RFI, or published full-depth vehicle trials. This test combines their separate capability goals with recovery and reuse. Six months comes from NOC's original ALR6000 design target at 6,000 m. It is not an externally agreed full-depth threshold.

milestones.title: Vehicle structures pass 1.2× service-pressure tests and equipment passes 1.1× tests.
milestones.criterion: Pressure structures pass strength and sealing tests at 1.2 times maximum service pressure; equipment passes chamber tests up to 1.1 times maximum service pressure. These are Dream Chaser's published qualification tests. Its integrated functional systems operated at full-ocean-depth pressure for 12 hours in laboratory tests reported on 14 June 2022; one vehicle system was described.
milestones.set_by: Shanghai Ocean University and Westlake University Dream Chaser team, laboratory qualification protocol in Section 3.1; these factors were published for that vehicle.
milestones.threshold_quote: with 1.2 times the maximum service pressure.

milestones.title: An AUV re-identifies a mapped seafloor site using stored visual landmarks.
milestones.criterion: An AUV returns to a mapped area and recognizes its stored distribution of seafloor features to localize itself. NASA/JPL specifies this Orpheus function; NOAA requires independent navigation ground truth but gives no numerical revisit-error limit. During EX-21-02, from 14 May to 27 May 2021, two AUVs completed eight deployments at 12–866 m. Recorded imagery supported feature tracking during playback. The expedition report does not establish autonomous site reacquisition.
milestones.set_by: NASA/JPL, published Orpheus visual-navigation objective; NOAA Ocean Exploration, EX-21-02 navigation-validation instructions. These objectives concern Orpheus.
milestones.threshold_quote: it will recognize the unique distribution of the features and use them as a starting point to expand its exploration.

milestones.title: An uncrewed vehicle completes a Challenger Deep seabed science dive in an 11,000 m-class sea trial.
milestones.criterion: An uncrewed vehicle reaches Challenger Deep's seabed, performs observation, mapping or sampling, and returns. Dream Chaser's protocol specifies an 11,000 m sea-trial stage; its 2020 trials reached 6,347 m. A paper published on 27 February 2024 reports eight Haidou-1 dives exceeding 10,000 m across three operating modes, reaching 10,908 m in the west pool and probing 10,909 m in the east pool. One Petrel-X PLUS completed three profiles exceeding 10,000 m in July 2020, reaching 10,619 m; its 2.018 km mean position deviation was measured at the surface.
milestones.set_by: Dream Chaser development team's staged sea-trial protocol, Section 5.2; its final stage concerns an 11,000 m-class vehicle. Haidou-1 and Petrel-X PLUS provide separate published results.

milestones.title: An 11,000 m-qualified AUV completes six months of mobile science at the Challenger Deep seabed.
milestones.criterion: An integrated AUV completes six months of scientific operation at the Challenger Deep seabed without servicing or continuous ship attendance, including movement between sites and autonomous reacquisition of a mapped site. This Atlas integration test extends NOC's six-month ALR6000 design target from 6,000 m to full depth. NOC's 2023 paper reports a separate, 1,500 m-rated vehicle's five-week, approximately 2,000 km unaccompanied deployment from 10 May to 13 June 2022. None of the cited results establishes the integrated six-month full-depth mission.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas; no published integrated full-depth endurance test was found. The duration comes from NOC's ALR6000 design target, which concerned a shallower vehicle.

not_found: No public standard, prize rule or agency acceptance test was found combining 11,000 m capability, seasonal endurance, site reacquisition, scientific return and reuse.
No common numerical acceptance limits were found for seafloor revisit error, minimum full-depth operating time or campaign reliability.
ARPA-E's 2022 marine-platform RFI uses 6,000 m for its full-ocean-depth scope and does not specify an 11,000 m endurance target.
Readable full text of the 2023 Petrel-X PLUS Ocean Engineering paper was not retrieved; its attributed 80-dive or 200-day design claim remains unverified.
Readable copies of the supplied 2018 Jamieson and 2024 Glud–Schauberger sources were not retrieved.

results.finding: In six revisit pairs at Site 1, AnyLoc achieved a mean Recall@1 of 24.9% on AUV imagery.
results.detail: The benchmark matched imagery from repeat AUV surveys against stored images using footprint-based ground truth. It does not establish that the AUV recognized the site or localized itself during a deployment.
results.quote: In particular, AnyLoc performs slightly better than MegaLoc on Site 1, achieving mean Recall@1 and Recall@10 of 24.9% and 51.2%, respectively, compared to 21.9% and 46.3% for MegaLoc.

results.finding: MOGLI gliders, number unspecified, patrolled the JONSIS Line for 21 months.
